extracted.intended_audience: patent attorneys, patent agents, law students, and inventors preparing patent filings
extracted.subtask_short: patent office proceedings and specification requirements
extracted.subtask_description: Rules and standards governing patent specifications, claims, caveats, filings, examinations, fees, and related Patent Office procedural requirements under 19th-century U.S. statute and case law. Covers what must be disclosed, oath and signature formalities, timing/abandonment, interfering applications, reissue limits, and required drawings/models/specimens.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims construed by substance (result vs means)
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims couched in words of result but in reality for the means or mechanism will be construed as claiming the means/mechanism rather than a mere result.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: A claim described as for the 'result' was held to be in words a claim for the result but in reality for the means or mechanism by which that result was to be attained; courts will look to substance over form when construing claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Combination claims must set forth general elements and arrangement
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim for a general combination consisting of several sub-combinations is valid where the general elements in combination and arrangement are set forth in the specification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: A sewing-machine claim comprising (1) mechanism for forming the stitch, (2) mechanism for holding cloth, (3) feeding mechanism was upheld because all these general elements and their arrangement were set forth in the specification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not over-emphasize machine vs. combination distinction
rubrics_metrics.description: Too much stress should not be laid upon the distinction between a machine and a combination; courts will construe according to the substance of the claim and specification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Court guidance warns against rigidly separating 'machine' from 'combination' when construing patent claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims describing constructed device are claims to the device itself
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim describing 'the manner of arranging and connecting' parts 'so as to accomplish the end proposed' may be construed as a claim to the constructed device itself; novelty of the whole device is not destroyed by prior use of individual parts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Winans claim construed as for the car itself constructed and arranged as in the patent; prior use of constituent parts did not impeach novelty of the combination/device.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reissue must not expand invention into abstraction or principle
rubrics_metrics.description: A reissue that attempts to convert an improved machine into an abstraction, principle, or mode of operation by using expanded or equivocal claims is an abuse and renders the reissue void.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge Grier: surrendering valid patents and obtaining reissued patents with expanded/equivocal claims where original was neither inoperative nor invalid is a 'great abuse' and injurious to the public.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims only cover what the specification describes (process vs arrangement)
rubrics_metrics.description: Where the specification describes an arrangement or configuration but not the process of performing it, the claim will not be held to cover the un-described process; it covers the arrangement/structure as described.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Booth v. Garelly — ornamental design claim covered arrangement of colored threads as producing ornamentation, not the unwritten winding process.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims to known parts apply only in combination/application
rubrics_metrics.description: If claim words describe 'the metal fixings and the mode of applying the same' and the fixings are notoriously old, the claim applies to the application/mode of applying them, not to the old parts standing alone.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Oxley v. Holden: old parts are not claimed apart from their novel application as described.

rubrics_metrics.name: Caveat contents requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: A caveat must set forth the design and purpose of the invention and its principal and distinguishing characteristics, and pray protection until the invention is matured.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Under the 1836 and 1870 acts, caveat contents are to be filed in the confidential archives and preserved in secrecy; fee required on filing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Caveat duration and notice/response procedure
rubrics_metrics.description: A caveat is operative for a term (one year under 1870 act); if another application is made within that term that may interfere, the commissioner deposits the other application's papers in confidential archives and must give notice by mail to the caveator, who then has three months (with mail transmission time added) to file description, specifications, drawings, and model to avail himself of the caveat.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: 1861/1870 statutory modifications: the three-month period is computed from deposit in Washington post-office plus usual transmission time (indorsed on notice). If specifications interfere, like proceedings as for interfering applications follow.

rubrics_metrics.name: Caveat as evidence of (lack of) perfection—not conclusive
rubrics_metrics.description: Filing a caveat is evidence that the invention was not perfected at that time but is not conclusive; the court will consider the caveat together with other parts of the instrument and other evidence to determine whether invention was perfected in law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Johnson v. Root: a caveat statement that the filer was 'making experiments to perfect' is evidence but not conclusive; jury may find that, in law, the invention was perfected despite a caveat.

rubrics_metrics.name: Application (petition) form and effect
rubrics_metrics.description: An application is made in writing by petition; the form is not material provided it sets forth the facts required by statute; the petition when filed is presumed to adopt the specification filed with it and asks for a patent for the described invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Patent Office rules give a recommended petition form (see Appendix); withdrawing and refiling under certain conditions may be treated as continuous application.

rubrics_metrics.name: Continuity of applications is a factual question
rubrics_metrics.description: If an applicant withdraws an application and later files a new petition intending continuity (e.g., paying forfeit and refiling), the two petitions may be treated as parts of the same continuous application; continuity is a jury question.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Godfrey v. Eames: whether transactions constitute continuity is for the jury to decide.

rubrics_metrics.name: Oath requirement: belief standard and contents
rubrics_metrics.description: Applicant must make oath or affirmation that he 'does verily believe' he is the original and first inventor/discoverer, that he does not know or believe the same was ever before known or used, and must state his citizenship.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Oath may be made before any authorized person in the U.S. or appropriate foreign official; statute requires belief rather than absolute knowledge; subsequent discovery of foreign prior use after oath does not invalidate patent in certain cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Oath irregularities cured by issuing patent; oath as evidentiary foundation
rubrics_metrics.description: An irregularity in form of the oath is cured by issuance of the patent; the taking of the oath is prerequisite to granting but not essential to validity once issued; however, when recited in the patent, the oath forms the foundation of the burden of proof on challengers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts have held patents valid despite some oath defects; but the recited oath shifts onus of proof in infringement/priority disputes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fees and discriminatory fee repeal (statutory fee schedule)
rubrics_metrics.description: The patent statutes prescribe fees for filing caveats, original applications, issuing patents, reissues, extensions, disclaimers, appeals, certified copies, recording assignments, and copies of drawings; acts of 1861 and 1870 reset many of these fees and abolished discriminatory rates against U.S. inhabitants.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: filing original application $15; issuing patent $20; filing caveat $10; fees for design patents vary by term (e.g., three years six months $10, seven years $15, fourteen years $30); detailed fee schedule in §68 and §75 of 1870 act.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specification enablement and best mode (section 26 of 1870)
rubrics_metrics.description: Specification must be a written description of the manner and process of making, constructing, compounding, and using the invention 'in such full, clear, concise, and exact terms' as to enable any person skilled in the art to make, construct, compound, and use it; in case of a machine, explain the principle and the best mode contemplated of applying that principle, so as to distinguish it from other inventions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Also requires particularly pointing out and distinctly claiming the part, improvement, or combination claimed; specification and claim must be signed by inventor and attested by two witnesses. This is statutory mandatory language.

rubrics_metrics.name: Drawings requirement and formalities
rubrics_metrics.description: Where the nature of the case admits of drawings, applicant must furnish one copy signed by the inventor or his attorney in fact and attested by two witnesses, to be filed in the Patent Office; a copy furnished by the Patent Office is to be attached to the patent as part of the specification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The rule applies 'when the nature of the case admits' of drawings; reasonable costs for copies of drawings are chargeable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Composition specimens when required
rubrics_metrics.description: For inventions that are compositions of matter, the applicant, if required by the commissioner, must furnish specimens of ingredients and of the composition sufficient in quantity for experimental purposes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Section 28 statutory requirement; useful for enabling examination of chemical or material inventions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Models when required
rubrics_metrics.description: In all cases which admit of representation by model, the applicant, if required by the commissioner, must furnish one of convenient size to exhibit advantageously the several parts of the invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Models help the Office and examiners understand mechanical inventions; requirement is discretionary with the commissioner.

rubrics_metrics.name: Commissioner's duty to examine and standard for issuing patent
rubrics_metrics.description: On filing application and payment of duty, the commissioner must cause examination; if it appears the claimant is justly entitled and the invention is sufficiently useful and important, the commissioner shall issue a patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This places substantive (entitlement) and utilitarian (useful and important) standards on the issuance decision.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timeliness and abandonment rule (two-year rule)
rubrics_metrics.description: All applications must be completed and prepared for examination within two years after filing the petition; failure to do so or to prosecute within two years after any action (with notice) results in the applications being regarded as abandoned unless Commissioner is satisfied delay was unavoidable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applicant must show unavoidable delay to avoid abandonment; statutory two-year default rule.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assignee application formalities and executor rights
rubrics_metrics.description: When an assignee seeks to obtain letters patent, the application and the specification must be sworn to by the inventor (and in case of reissue if inventor living); if inventor dies, right devolves to executor/administrator and oath form is varied so legal representatives may make it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exception for patents issued and assigned prior to July 8, 1870; statutory provision governs post-1870 cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Renewing or re-filing after failure to pay final fee or prior rejection
rubrics_metrics.description: A person who failed to pay the final fee within six months after allowance may apply for a patent as in an original application provided the second application is made within two years after allowance; applicants whose applications were rejected or withdrawn before the act may have six months from the act passage to renew or file anew; abandonment remains a question of fact at hearing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Section 35 and related provisions set out deadlines and protections for renewed filings and prevent damages for manufacture/use before issue in certain circumstances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Notification and assistance when claim rejected
rubrics_metrics.description: When a claim is rejected on examination, the commissioner must notify the applicant briefly stating reasons for rejection and provide information and references useful in judging whether to renew the application or alter the specification; if applicant persists, the commissioner must order re-examination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Statutory duty to give reasons and helpful references; persistence triggers re-examination procedures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interfering applications and priority determination
rubrics_metrics.description: If an application would, in the commissioner's opinion, interfere with a pending application or an unexpired patent, the commissioner shall give notice and direct the primary examiner to determine priority of invention; commissioner may issue to the adjudged prior inventor unless adverse appeal is taken within prescribed time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Formalized interference procedure with right to appeal from examiner decisions; notice and priority determination are statutory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent signatures and countersignature
rubrics_metrics.description: Patents shall be issued in the name of the United States under the seal of the office and signed by the Secretary of the Interior and countersigned by the Commissioner of Patents (post-1849/1870 statutory allocation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Formal signing/countersigning requirement reflects statutory supervision changes (Secretary of State earlier; Secretary of Interior after 1849/1870).

rubrics_metrics.name: Reissue abuse doctrine (factual standard)
rubrics_metrics.description: Surrendering valid patents and obtaining reissues with expanded or equivocal claims where the original patent was neither inoperative nor invalid and the specification neither defective nor insufficient is an abuse of the reissue privilege and the reissue is void.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Case law (Burr v. Duryee / Judge Grier) condemns reissues that expand protection to cover prior/future inventions by elastic phrasing; courts will invalidate such reissues.
